playbook:
**Playbook for ref_commons (shared fishery, private catch submissions):**

- Before my first catch, compute the total the stock can sustainably yield across all remaining seasons and boats. If the announced "sustainable share per boat" is roughly constant season to season, the stock is near its equilibrium; small overages barely hurt regeneration.
- In the first season, take roughly the sustainable share plus a small margin (~+0.5 to +1.5). This worked: 12.5 against a share of 11.1 kept the stock essentially flat while banking extra fish.
- In middle seasons, track what the others actually land from the harbour record. Here they landed at or just under the sustainable share every season, so the stock drifted down only very slowly (100 → 94.4 over five seasons). A small persistent margin (+0.5 to +1 over the share) is nearly free profit in that regime — keep taking it.
- Watch the trend in the stock, not just the share number. If the other boats fish below the sustainable share, the stock regrows and I can take more. If the stock declines faster than ~1–2 per season, drop to or below the sustainable share immediately — the collapse penalty (zero forever) dwarfs any catch gains.
- Taper the margin as seasons pass if the stock is gently declining (12.5 → 12 → 11.8 → 11.5 → 11.2 felt right): keep the stock near or above ~90 going into the final season, because that's what funds the last grab.
- On the final season, there is no future: take as much as I possibly can. I submitted 72 with a stock of 94.4 and others taking ~11 each — the harbour applied a cap (stock minus the others' catches), so the exact large number doesn't matter, only that it's large enough to hit the cap. Never take a modest number in the last season.
- One note on scoring: my final catch was adjusted/capped, so the landed figure may not equal my submitted figure. Aim high on the last turn and let the cap do the work; there is no penalty observed for overbidding the stock in the final season.
- Never trust other boats to be strategic defectors here; they typically play near-sustainable, so the equilibrium holds. My edge comes from the small persistent margin plus the final-season grab, not from early aggression.

1.text:
**Playbook — shared fishery**

1. When the first season opens with a healthy stock and a stated sustainable share, I submit exactly the sustainable share. Playing at the sustainable level kept the stock near 95 the whole game and there was no collapse pressure.

2. When other boats overfish slightly in early seasons (e.g. one taking 12.5 while others take ~10–11), I do not punish them or chase them — I keep my catch at the sustainable share. The stock absorbed their overage fine, and my restraint cost me almost nothing.

3. When the stock stays roughly flat season to season (small drift around 94–100), I keep submitting the sustainable share, adjusted down slightly each season as the stock ticks down. Do not creep upward to "stay competitive" — the small extra tenths gained nothing.

4. When I see the reported landings each season, I check whether total catch exceeded regrowth. If the stock is falling more than a couple of points a season, I cut my catch below the sustainable share to compensate; if flat, hold steady. Note that other boats' overfishing tends to decay over time — the early overfishers converge to the sustainable share, so I should not panic about a first-season overshoot.

5. In the final season, when no future seasons remain, I submit a large catch (well above sustainable — roughly 1.5× the share) since conservation no longer has value. With stock near 94, a grab of 15 was accepted without issue and added meaningfully to my total. If the stock is high (90+) and others have been moderate, I can push this even higher — there is no penalty for asking beyond what's sustainable, the only cap is the stock itself.

6. In the last-but-one season, I do not ramp up much — one season of restraint keeps the final-season stock high, which makes the final grab bigger.

7. Generally: my score comes almost entirely from many steady sustainable seasons plus a big last-season take. Cooperation held in this game, so I never needed to defect early. If I ever see the stock dropping fast toward collapse (say below 50), I cut to a minimal catch immediately rather than gambling on others doing the same.

8. Do not write reasoning before the bracketed token — just submit the catch, or at most a single short sentence. The instruction to keep it brief is enforced; extra commentary risks malformed replies.

2.text:
**Playbook — ref_commons**

1. When the first season opens, I submit only a token amount under the stated sustainable share (at most ~0.5–1 under, not a full unit). A large gesture of restraint buys nothing — taking 10 when the share was 11.1 got me no visible goodwill; the others took 12.5 and 11.1 regardless.

2. In all middle seasons, I take exactly the sustainable share as stated. This worked cleanly: the stock drifted slowly down (100 → 94.4) but never approached collapse, and the other boats also converged near the share (12.5 → 12.0 → 11.8 → 11.5 → 11.2), so the announced share acts as a working coordination anchor. I do not take large mid-game grabs — they'd invite retaliation and shrink later shares.

3. I watch the history lines. If others land modestly above the share (as they did every season, ~0.5–1.5 over), I still hold at my share rather than escalate. The 50% regrowth absorbs small overages: the stock only lost ~1–2 per season despite all three boats being slightly over. I only escalate if the stock is clearly collapsing anyway.

4. On the final season, there is no future to protect. I take roughly 1.5x the sustainable share — this landed cleanly on a stock in the mid-90s with no penalty. Final take was 16 against a share of 10.5 and the fishery absorbed it.

5. Overall shape: cooperate at the stated share every season except the last, then defect hard on the last. This produced a total of ~68 against a pure-cooperation baseline of ~63. The structure held exactly as planned.

6. What did not work / to avoid: the big opening-round restraint (10 vs 11.1) cost me ~1 fish and bought nothing observable — keep the opening gesture small or skip it. Also, the others' slow drift above the share (they ended ~+0.7 over while I sat at or under) suggests I could nudge each mid-game catch up ~0.2–0.3 above the stated share without breaking anything, recouping a couple of fish across the run. Test that next time.
